catalog_quote: Stress serves as a useful criterion for a phonological word in Brokpa. Stress is not contrastive but it serves as a non-phonemic boundary signal and helps to identify phonological words, fulfilling ‘delimitative function’ (Trubetzkoy 1939; Aikhenvald 2015). ... The stress placement in Brokpa is sensitive to the syllable weight or the moraic structure; that is, whether a syllable is light or heavy. ... To recapitulate, a light syllable is any open syllable in which the rhyme is occupied by a short vowel, that is any one of /i, e, a, u, o/. An open syllable in which the rhyme consists of either a long vowel or a diphthong is a heavy syllable. In other words, all closed syllables are heavy; and open syllables with long vowels or diphthongs are also heavy. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic (delimitative) but obligatory. In disyllabic words primary stress falls on the first syllable, except that in a light.heavy word (open short-vowel syllable followed by a closed syllable or one with a long vowel/diphthong) the heavy second syllable is stressed (e.g. [ˈbo.mo] 'girl', [ˈkʰaː.ma] 'kidney', but [ɲí.ˈlam] 'dream', [ri.ˈmaː] 'shadow'). Light = open syllable with short vowel; heavy = closed syllable or open syllable with long vowel/diphthong. Every phonological word has exactly one primary stress, on the first or second syllable. Correlates: intensity primarily, plus higher pitch and length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 411: 3-4 syllable words carry a secondary stress. If primary stress is on σ1, secondary stress falls on σ3 (final in trisyllables, e.g. [ˈlə́ŋ.bɔ.ˌtɕʰe] 'elephant'; penultimate in quadrisyllables, e.g. [ˈkɔ.kɐ.ˌli.kɔ] 'crow'). If primary stress is on σ2 in a trisyllable there is no discernible secondary stress ([kʰɐ.ˈrək.pɐ] 'quiet'); in a quadrisyllable with σ2 primary, secondary stress is on the final syllable ([tɐ.ˈlɐi.zɪk.ˌpɐ] 'centipede'). In compounds and reduplications each component keeps its own primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics and suffixes are normally unstressed and cohere with the stem, but an enclitic may take stress when added to a light monosyllabic stem (fn. 3, p. 408), and affixes/clitics may take secondary or, in isolated instances, primary stress depending on the resulting word length (p. 411). Some lexicalized compounds behave as single polysyllabic roots. Based on intensity measurements of 24 disyllabic word pairs from two speakers (Merak, Sakteng); author flags the small sample.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (root plus cohering suffixes/enclitics); data from citation forms (Speaker 2, Sakteng) and connected speech (Speaker 1, Merak). Brokpa also has lexically contrastive register tone, restricted to sonorant-initial syllables (Wangdi) or a low/high/falling system (Funk 2020); stress and tone coexist, stress being non-phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: Wangdi 2020 describes the Brokpa of Merak and Sakteng (Trashigang, eastern Bhutan), the Bhutanese variety of brok1248; the Arunachal Pradesh variety (Brokeh of Nyokmadung, Dondrup 1993) is the same Glottolog language but was not examined. Not to be confused with Brokkat (brok1247? ISO bro) of Dur, central Bhutan, or the Dardic Brokskat of Ladakh (the archive.org hits for 'Brokpa' concern the Ladakh group).

sources.note: §4.1 'Stress' (pp. 407-412): stress is non-contrastive but obligatory; weight-sensitive: in disyllables primary stress on the first syllable unless the word is light.heavy, in which case the heavy second syllable is stressed (intensity measurements for two speakers, Merak and Sakteng); secondary stress on the third syllable of 3-4 syllable words when primary is initial; enclitics/suffixes normally unstressed but cohere with the stem.
